title: How To Give Everyday People A Say In AI Governance | NOEMA
gist: Landemore argues that elite AI-governance statements — including July's 200-signatory 'We Must Act Now' and the 'AI 2027' and 'Europe 2031' forecasts — systematically exclude the public, and proposes a three-tier fix: an LLM-mediated global consultation running on ChatGPT/Gemini/Meta AI's billion-user reach within months, then AI-facilitated online deliberation, then citizens' assemblies feeding a global assembly. She names concrete lab precedents (Anthropic's 1,000-American constitution and 81,000-user survey, OpenAI's Democratic Inputs, Meta's Community Forums) and proposes compute and chip-supply access as the enforcement lever.

themes.theme: The missing public in elite AI governance

insights.claim: The July statement 'We Must Act Now,' signed by more than 200 economists and AI researchers including 17 Nobel laureates, is four sentences long and convokes only economists, policymakers and technology leaders, with society appearing once as a beneficiary rather than a participant.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: The elite consensus on AI risk is explicitly technocratic; expect governance proposals designed without public-input mechanisms and the legitimacy backlash that follows.
insights.quote: The statement convokes economists, policymakers and technology leaders alone.
insights.locator: All of it is true. What is remarkable

insights.claim: 'AI 2027,' published April 2025 by the AI Futures Project, gives a month-by-month account of a race to superintelligence running to late 2027 with a real chance of catastrophic loss of human control, treating the public as a population to be protected rather than consulted.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Names the specific forecast document anchoring policy urgency and its implicit timeline — useful for dating expected regulatory action.
insights.locator: “AI 2027,” a widely read essay published

insights.claim: 'Europe 2031,' published in June, finds Europe holds 5% of global compute and one frontier lab, with regulators not even allowed to use the tools they regulate, and gives the region until the end of the summer to turn its AI policy around or face assured technological and economic irrelevance within a few years.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A hard, quantified bear case on European AI positioning — 5% of compute and a single frontier lab is the number to carry into any EU tech allocation view.
insights.quote: The region, with 5% of global compute, one frontier lab and regulators who are not even allowed to use the tools they’re supposed to regulate
insights.locator: “Europe 2031,” a similar five-year forecast

insights.claim: Doomism and competitiveness anxiety are terrible organizing principles for AI policy; what actually mobilizes people is a positive story about what AI is for, told in the terms of their work, kids and towns and that they helped write.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Predicts safety-by-fear and sovereignty-by-panic campaigns underperform politically — relevant to how durable any AI regulation actually proves.
insights.quote: Doomism and competitiveness anxiety are terrible organizing principles.
insights.locator: Doomism and competitiveness anxiety

themes.theme: AI platforms as unprecedented deliberative infrastructure

insights.claim: OpenAI reported 900 million weekly active ChatGPT users in February and crossed a billion monthly users in June; Google's Gemini went from 400 million to more than 900 million monthly active users on a similar timeline; and Meta AI also reported a billion monthly users.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Three independent billion-scale AI distribution points reached within months of each other — the clearest available read on consumer AI reach parity.
insights.locator: Our only plausible option to achieve this

insights.claim: No government, broadcaster or international body has ever had standing two-way contact with such a huge portion of humanity simultaneously, which makes frontier AI CEOs — not elected leaders — the actors best placed to facilitate a genuine global deliberation.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Frames platform reach as quasi-sovereign civic infrastructure; strengthens the political case for treating frontier labs as regulated utilities.
insights.quote: the people best placed to actually facilitate a global deliberation on AI may not be elected leaders and heads of governments, but the heads of the companies building this technology
insights.locator: This is a strange but real option

insights.claim: The infrastructure to ask hundreds of millions of people the same question in the same week already exists, so a global public consultation run primarily online is the only format fast enough given the compressed timelines.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Turns distribution scale into a governance asset — a differentiator labs could deploy pre-emptively to shape regulation.
insights.quote: The infrastructure to ask hundreds of millions of people or more the same question in the same week already exists.
insights.locator: Using these companies’ best models to ask

insights.claim: Tier one, an LLM-mediated global consultation, could produce an interim draft within months: a minimal, broadly endorsed statement of what a large fraction of the world wants AI to do and never do.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: The fastest concrete governance artifact on offer — months, not years — and the one labs could unilaterally fund.
insights.locator: The first tier, an LLM-mediated global consultation

insights.claim: A well-run consultation should be broken out by region rather than flattened into a global average, because preferences genuinely diverge — for example between a Western emphasis on individual data privacy and precautionary restriction and a data-sovereignty, development-first framing more common in Africa and India.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Names the actual fault line in global AI rules: precaution versus development-first data sovereignty — the split that will shape divergent regional regimes.
insights.locator: Run well, this tier would need not flatten

insights.claim: Tier two would be an online global deliberation in which participants interact with each other in real time mediated by AI facilitators, producing a richer text that tests and sometimes replaces the LLM-aggregated recommendations.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Defines a product category — AI facilitation of mass deliberation — that does not commercially exist yet.
insights.locator: The second tier would be more logistically demanding

insights.claim: Tier three would run local and national citizens' assemblies plus referenda in every country, feeding a concluding global citizens' assembly that could ratify, amend or supersede the earlier floors as time allows.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A deliberately fail-safe design: if the AI timeline is short you still hold a floor, if it is long the slower tiers take over.
insights.quote: If the clock turns out to be as short as feared, we would not be left with nothing.
insights.locator: The third tier would reach deeper still

insights.claim: The machinery for the deepest tier already exists and has been tested — Ireland's citizens' assemblies and France's Citizens' Convention on Climate — and lacks only a mandate at the scale of the moment.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Proof the institutional technology is off-the-shelf; the binding constraint is political will and funding, not method.
insights.locator: The machinery for the third tier exists

insights.claim: An investigation by The Economist comparing the apparent values of 25 frontier AI models to the World Values Survey found the models often hold values more extreme than the average respondent across the 88 countries surveyed — in some cases more secular or individualist than any society on Earth — and tend to compress the world's moral diversity.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Hard evidence of systematic cultural skew in frontier models — a concrete product and regulatory risk in non-Western markets.
insights.quote: the models often hold values more extreme than the average respondent in the 88 countries surveyed by the WVS
insights.locator: A recent investigation by The Economist

insights.claim: A single model producing a single constitutional draft leaves one artifact, one process and one set of justifications all traceable to the lab that built it, with no independent adversarial record; a team of models in dialogue would at least leave a trail of positions taken and abandoned.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: An auditability design principle: multi-model adversarial process as the substitute for institutional checks — a plausible requirement future regulation adopts.
insights.locator: Another worry with a constitution mediated

insights.claim: Every constitutional tradition now treated as legitimate began from an exclusion at least as serious as the one an AI-mediated consultation would carry — most early democratic constitutions were written by men, for men — and were corrected over time rather than voided.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: The author's pre-emptive rebuttal to the legitimacy objection; signals she expects the fight over representativeness, not feasibility.
insights.quote: We did not retroactively void those constitutions; we built on them and corrected the exclusion over time.
insights.locator: But every constitutional tradition we now treat

themes.theme: Direct asks to frontier labs and their track records

insights.claim: In 2023 Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project sourced constitutional principles from roughly 1,000 ordinary Americans and trained a real model on them, finding less biased outputs in some areas than the standard internally authored model — evidence that public input can improve a model, not just legitimize it.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A measurable performance argument for participatory alignment, which makes public input a product decision rather than a PR one.
insights.quote: This is evidence that public input doesn’t just confer legitimacy, it can make a model better.
insights.locator: To Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic

insights.claim: In 2025 Anthropic used an AI interviewer to survey nearly 81,000 Claude users across 159 countries and 70 languages in a single week, demonstrating that mass AI-mediated consultation is already operationally proven.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Concrete throughput benchmark for AI-mediated consultation — 81,000 people, 159 countries, one week.
insights.locator: In 2025, Anthropic used an AI interviewer

insights.claim: Anthropic's new Constitution for Claude, published in January, was written the same closed way as the old one — a small internal team with the model itself and a handful of outside experts, but not the tens of millions of people who now use it.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Names the gap between labs' participatory research and their actual governance practice — an obvious pressure point for critics and regulators.
insights.quote: What’s missing isn’t proof of concept. It’s the will to use it.
insights.locator: In January, Anthropic published a new

insights.claim: OpenAI's 2023 Democratic Inputs to AI program funded 10 teams selected from nearly 1,000 applicants to prototype public-input methods, but never amounted to anything close to what OpenAI's reach could support.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A documented pattern of pilot-and-abandon at frontier labs; discount announced governance initiatives accordingly.
insights.locator: To Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI

insights.claim: Meta's 2022 Community Forum on Cyberbullying in the Metaverse, run with Stanford's Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Behavioral Insights Team, gathered input from nearly 6,500 people across 32 countries, and its 2023 and 2024 forums on generative AI each drew more than 1,000 participants from the West and the Global South.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Existing corporate deliberation precedent at meaningful scale — the template a standing global institution would be built on.
insights.locator: To Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta

insights.claim: A global AI constitution would bind like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights — unenforceable by any court but accruing weight over decades as principles governments invoke, NGOs cite and states pay a reputational price for flouting.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations: soft law with compounding norm value, not treaty enforcement.
insights.locator: A global AI constitution produced on the basis

insights.claim: Defection would be made costly through exclusion from joint safety research, from preferential compute or chip-supply arrangements, and from the diplomatic credibility of taking AI risk seriously.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Compute and chip access proposed explicitly as the enforcement lever for AI governance — a direct channel from governance politics to semiconductor allocation.
insights.quote: exclusion from joint safety research, from preferential compute or chip-supply arrangements and from the diplomatic credibility that comes with taking the technology’s risks seriously
insights.locator: Defection or refusal to participate would be costly

insights.claim: Corporate infrastructure alone is insufficient: citizens' assemblies and referenda require official standing, public funding and a commitment to act, with the U.N. positioned as convener of the concluding global assembly and guarantor that a lab-initiated process does not end up owned by labs.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Defines the hand-off point where AI governance moves from private to public control — the contested boundary to watch.
insights.locator: And to governments and the United Nations

insights.claim: Noema discloses that the initial draft of the piece used Claude as an editorial assistant for brainstorming and pressure-testing claims but not to originate facts, followed by multiple human edits, identity verification, scanners and a detailed human fact-check.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: An emerging disclosure standard for AI-assisted publishing — a template media companies will be pushed to match.
